title: Iran Claims Strikes Destroyed US Patriot Systems and Radar at Gulf Bases
excerpt: Tehran says IRGC attacks hit air defense systems, early-warning radar and satellite communications at US military installations in Kuwait, as the conflict enters its second week with mounting American casualties.
body:
• Iran's IRGC claims it destroyed Patriot missile defense systems, early-warning radar and satellite communication infrastructure at US bases in Kuwait
  • The US-Iran conflict has entered its second week, with 18 American service members killed and nearly 450 wounded since fighting resumed on July 7
  • Pentagon officials fear Russia and China may be helping Iran improve its missile targeting capabilities after strikes penetrated US air defenses

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed this week that its missile and drone attacks struck and destroyed key components of US air defense infrastructure at military bases in Kuwait and Jordan, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency. The IRGC said its forces hit Patriot missile defense systems, early-warning radar, missile defense radar and satellite communication systems at Ahmad Al Jaber Air Base in Kuwait.

Iranian state media separately circulated what it described as satellite imagery showing "extensive damage" to the US AN/FPS-117 early-warning radar system at Ali Al-Salem Air Base, also in Kuwait. US Central Command has declined to comment on battle damage from the Iranian attacks, according to the New York Post.

The IRGC said the strikes were intended to neutralize regional radar surveillance ahead of further missile and drone operations against US positions, according to Madhyamam Online.

A War Grinding Into Its Second Week

The exchange of fire between the US and Iran has now stretched past 12 consecutive days, with US Central Command conducting nightly strikes on Iranian military targets including command centers, maritime capabilities, missile launch sites and air defense systems across Iran's southern coast. US strikes have targeted sites in Sirik, Bandar Abbas, Qeshm Island, Chabahar and Konarak, according to Reuters.

The fighting resumed in early July after Iran attacked commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, which the White House described as a violation of a June memorandum of understanding. US strikes have since expanded to include bridges, airports, ports and energy infrastructure.

"Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!"

— President Donald Trump, Truth Social post, July 21

The conflict, dubbed Operation Epic Fury by the Pentagon, has now claimed 18 American lives. On July 17, an Iranian ballistic missile struck prefabricated housing units at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, killing three US troops identified as 1st Lt. Tyler J. Feehan of Hawaii, Pvt. Isabella Gonzales of Texas and Army Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad of New York. A fourth service member was killed in Iraq during the controlled detonation of a downed Iranian drone, the Wall Street Journal reported. Nearly 450 US troops have been wounded since July 7, though the Pentagon says 96% have returned to duty.

Fears of Russian and Chinese Assistance

Iran's increasingly precise strikes have fueled concerns within the Pentagon that Tehran is receiving targeting assistance from Russia and China. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth confirmed Tuesday that Moscow and Beijing are providing "some level of support" to Iran, though he said the extent remains classified.

American intelligence officials are investigating whether Russia helped Iran improve its ability to strike sensitive US targets, including CIA facilities in the Gulf, through advanced drone technology and targeting assistance, Reuters reported. A Western intelligence assessment concluded Russia likely played a role in targeting regional CIA facilities, while Gulf officials said analysts believed a Saudi strike involved two Russian-enhanced versions of Iran's Shahed drones.

"Iran appears to have altered its tactics and has learned from missile defense capabilities during previous rounds of conflict just as it did when striking Israel. Combine that with intelligence support from near-peer competitors, and it can lead to deadly outcomes."

— Alex Plitsas, Atlantic Council senior fellow and former Pentagon official

Gulf Allies Under Fire

The IRGC's attacks have extended well beyond US military installations. Iranian strikes hit Kuwaiti power generation and water desalination plants on Monday, causing fires and disrupting electricity generation. Kuwait's Ministry of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy described the attacks as "heinous Iranian aggression." Repairs were underway by Tuesday, authorities said.

In Bahrain, the IRGC said it targeted infrastructure belonging to Amazon and accommodation facilities used by US military personnel at Sheikh Isa Air Base. Jordan said its forces intercepted and destroyed five Iranian drones targeting its territory. None of these claims have been independently verified.

The maritime front has also intensified. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency confirmed that a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile, forcing its crew to abandon the vessel and board lifeboats. Just four commodity vessels crossed the strait on Monday, down from seven the previous day, according to Kpler data. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have threatened a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, potentially putting two of the world's most vital energy arteries at risk.

Implications for the Indian Diaspora

The escalating hostilities carry direct consequences for the estimated eight million Indians living and working across the Gulf states. Strikes on Kuwaiti civilian infrastructure, including water and power facilities, raise immediate quality-of-life concerns for Indian workers in the country. The US State Department has issued a global security advisory warning of heightened risks, travel disruptions, flight cancellations and airspace closures across the Middle East.

Oil markets have so far been kept in check by reports of diplomatic efforts, with Brent crude at $88.87 per barrel. But a full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait could reduce global oil supply by 7%, a scenario that would hit India — the world's third-largest oil importer — especially hard.

Diplomatic Efforts Continue

Despite the escalation, mediation efforts have not collapsed entirely. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had received a proposal from mediators for a 10-day ceasefire aimed at salvaging the interim deal that was intended to pave the way to a lasting agreement. Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni has asked Pakistan to resume its mediation role, arriving in Islamabad for talks this week.

The war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran, has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon. Israel has not joined the latest round of strikes. Former US envoy Keith Kellogg said he believes Russia is "primarily helping with targeting," while a regional source told the New York Post that China would prefer to see the war ended rather than expanded.
nri_angle: Escalating strikes on Gulf infrastructure and maritime routes directly threaten millions of Indian workers in the region and India's oil-dependent economy.
